newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metalworkers near deal in Hesse region.
newsitem.headline: German metalworkers near deal in Hesse region.

text.p: German metal and engineering trade union officials said on Wednesday they were confident of securing an acceptable pay deal for the some 400,000 workers in the regions of Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and the Saar.

Following an agreement signed earlier for some 600,000 workers in the southern region of Nordwuerttemberg, the new accord would mean wage deals have been signed for virtually all of the 3.2 million workers in Germany's metal and engineering sectors.

Moreover, all of the regional deals signed so far fail to implement a new law cutting sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, an issue which has provoked mass protests in the industry and led to threats of all-out strikes next year.

A spokesman for the IG Metall trade union in Frankfurt, where joint negotiations for the Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and the Saar regions are being held, said on Wednesday that negotiators were now very near to an agreement.

Both union and employer negotiators were said to be discussing a package similar to the break-through deal signed in the northern state of Lower Saxony earlier this month, which secured full sick pay for workers in return for cuts to bonuses.
Earlier in Stuttgart, metal and engineering employers in Nordwuerttemberg said they had agreed a 1997 wage deal for the some 600,000 workers in the industry there.
The accord mirrored the Lower Saxony deal in that workers will receive a 1.5 pay rise in 1997 and a further 2.5 percent increase the year after.
In return for allowing sick pay to be retained at 100 percent of salary, companies will be allowed to make small cuts in other areas, such as existing holiday or Christmas bonuses.

While such a package means that overall labour costs in the metal and engineering sectors will rise by less than one percent next year, it means that yet again employers will have failed to make the cost reductions they have for years been crying out for.
Wage talks in the German construction industry also began in Frankfurt but were also not expected to reach agreement today.
The union IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt has said one of its key objectives is to battle seasonal unemployment which soared to 400,000 workers last winter.
"We will not even come close to nearing an agreement today," Klaus Wiesehuegel, head of the union said.
